title: Program critique #1 (Upper Lower Push Pull)
summary: First subscriber program critique: a 4-day 5/3/1-based upper/lower/push/pull program from a lifter with two years' training, a 225 lb bench and bad shoulders who wants a 'bear mode' look. He keeps the template and 5/3/1 main lifts but adds back-off variation sets, raises accessory volume (5x10 rows and RDLs), adds shrugs, Coan rows, deficit deadlifts, chin-ups, push-ups, band pull-aparts and ab work, and organises nearly everything into supersets.

claims.claim: His program critiques are always from a hypertrophy standpoint, not strength or athletic performance.
A 4-day program run on an 8-day window (one day on, one day off) is fine.
He runs an 8-day rotation of day variations himself and trains every day, but doesn't advise others to train daily; it works for him.
When sending a program to critique, you must state your injuries; it is critical information for programming.
A 'bear mode' goal (big back, traps, yoke, shoulders, chest) requires shrugs and more row variations to build upper back size.
When critiquing he keeps the lifter's template and style unless asked to change it; your style of lifting is yours.
For most people wanting more chest he'd simply prescribe more benching, but with bad shoulders horizontal pressing is stressful, so bench volume stays limited.
5/3/1 alone lacks volume; add four back-off/variation sets after the main lift, e.g. close-grip bench or football/Swiss bar press.
Superset pressing variation sets with pull-ups: more work done, good for conditioning, pressing strength isn't hurt, and it keeps shoulders healthy.
Don't superset the 5/3/1 main sets; stay fresh and focused on them.
Overhead press 4x8 is a good choice for someone with bad shoulders; if you stagnate or regress, change the rep scheme (lower or higher reps, e.g. 6x2 or 5x10).
Overhead press can be superset with light band face pulls, depending on how much the press taxes your rear delts.
He is a fanatic of supersets.
For yoke, raise Pendlay rows from 3x10 to 5x10 and after each set deadlift the same bar back up and do AMRAP shrugs: five sets of shrugs with no extra equipment.

Biceps and triceps long head are the most appropriate muscles to train on a lower-body day; he would never train lateral/medial triceps or shoulders on lower day because they are injury-prone and need warming up.
5/3/1 squat is far too little squat volume; add a squat variation for four sets afterward (front, pause or safety bar squat).
RDL 3x10 isn't enough; do 5x10 superset with pull-ups for a big back.
He does his pull-ups as AMRAP sets and thinks doing as many as you can each time is good.
Superset biceps curls and skull crushers, and with bad shoulders add band pull-aparts to keep the rear delts warm.
Instead of resting between calf sets, do ab work.
If you change the 4x8 OHP rep scheme on a 5/3/1 program, lean toward higher reps since 5/3/1 already covers low reps.
With bad shoulders, dips are usually worse for the shoulders than bench; push-ups are a better alternative.
With bad shoulders the shoulders limit the bench, so pecs may be under-recruited; supersetting chest flies with paused bench helps fully recruit the chest.
Push-ups are amazing for the shoulder; if normal push-ups hurt, do close-grip (diamond) push-ups.
You don't need to rest between sets of lateral raises or triceps pushdowns; superset them with push-ups or chin-ups.
Chin-ups on push day add upper back and biceps work and keep the shoulders healthy; anyone wanting 'bear mode' should do them.
RDLs aren't a pull from the floor; add deficit deadlifts (4 sets of 8-12, light) after 5/3/1 sumo, superset with pull-ups, for a second floor pull.
Properly done Pendlay rows are strict with an uncontrolled negative, so no stretch at the bottom; Coan/cheat rows (cheat up, control the negative) stretch the back, important for yoke.
Don't put heavy Coan rows on deadlift day since the lower back is already fatigued; place them on upper day at 3x10-12, superset with dumbbell shrugs because the row weight is too heavy to shrug.
Biceps curls and face pulls can be paired in the same set since curls don't need rest.
Without back problems and with plenty of pull-ups for spinal decompression, a bear-mode program doesn't need hyperextensions.
Isolate the abs twice in four sessions, not for a six-pack but because the core is that important; it takes five minutes.
After good strength numbers, the next step is more and more volume; adjust rep schemes for more volume rather than adding new exercises, and reassess in about eight months.
He distinguishes program reviews (popular methods like 5/3/1) from critiques (programs sent by viewers, harsher and modified for hypertrophy); he prefers programs viewers made themselves.
